1. Core Clinical Tension: A pediatric renal transplant recipient on triple immunosuppression presents with fever, asthenia, and a cavitary pulmonary consolidation with mediastinal adenopathy, creating an urgent differential between bacterial pneumonia, invasive aspergillosis, and mycobacterial disease in the setting of a negative tuberculin test.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission phase ends following physical exam, baseline hematology/biochemistry, chest radiography, and thoracic CT. Gastric aspirates, tuberculin testing, and bronchoscopy with BAL constitute confirmatory diagnostic investigations.
3. Differential Distinctions: Bacterial pneumonia typically responds rapidly to beta-lactams; pulmonary aspergillosis demonstrates angioinvasive fungal hyphae; tuberculin skin tests may be falsely negative due to immunosuppressive therapy. Tuberculosis is confirmed by mycobacterial isolation on bronchoalveolar lavage.
case_prompt: A 13-year-old male was admitted with a one-week history of fever and asthenia. He had end-stage renal failure attributed to vesicoureteral reflux and had undergone a second deceased-donor renal transplantation three months previously. His maintenance immunosuppressive regimen comprised prednisone 10 mg/day, mycophenolate mofetil 1500 mg/day, and cyclosporine 75 mg twice daily, with adequate allograft function. On admission, the patient was asthenic with a temperature of 38.5°C, blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate of 90 beats/min, and inspiratory rhonchi with decreased breath sounds over both lung bases. There was no peripheral lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Initial laboratory testing showed hematocrit 38%, white blood cell count 8,300/mm³, platelet count 220,000/mm³, blood urea nitrogen 6.8 mmol/L, serum creatinine 75 µmol/L, C-reactive protein 88.5 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 51 mm/h. Serum protein electrophoresis showed total protein 65 g/L (albumin 33.9 g/L, alpha-1 5.8 g/L, alpha-2 9.6 g/L, beta-1 3.9 g/L, beta-2 3.4 g/L, gamma-globulin 8.3 g/L). Chest radiography revealed opacity in the right middle zone and superior mediastinal enlargement, and thoracic CT confirmed cavitary pneumonia of the right lower lobe with anterior mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute febrile respiratory illness with pulmonary consolidation and elevated inflammatory markers in an immunosuppressed host suggested typical or atypical bacterial pneumonia, but cavitary progression and persistent fevers prompted invasive evaluation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: three diagnoses were suspected: pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis and pulmonary aspergillosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Invasive fungal infection is a leading cause of cavitary lung lesions in solid organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy, but bronchoscopic microbiological workup revealed mycobacteria rather than fungal pathogens.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: three diagnoses were suspected: pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis and pulmonary aspergillosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Despite a negative tuberculin skin test (secondary to immunosuppressive anergy) and negative gastric aspirates, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid demonstrated Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fully susceptible to first-line agents.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: the diagnosis was made by the study of sputum specimens aspirated during bronchoalveolar lavage that revealed the presence of mycobacterium tuberculosis.
